title: Integrated Transcriptome-Metabolome Analysis of Rps2-A226Y Mutant Liver
text: Mammalian liver coordinates glucose, lipid and amino-acid metabolism, which makes it a sensible tissue for asking how a body-wide proteostatic stress shows up in metabolism. This post looks at liver transcriptomics and metabolomics from female Rps2-A226Y knock-in mice, which carry a ribosomal ambiguity mutation that increases missense mistranslation, compared with Cre-expressing wild-type controls. The mutant allele is expressed mosaically, and the mutant transcript accounts for roughly a quarter of liver Rps2 mRNA, so effect sizes should be read as diluted relative to the full mutant effect. Sample ages are reported as recorded in the metadata and are being checked against the animal records. This analysis is my part of a PhD project carried out between 2020 and 2022.

title: Integrated Transcriptome-Metabolome Analysis of Rps2-A226Y Mutant Liver
text:
Why This Analysis
This post summarizes an integrated liver omics analysis in female mice carrying Rps2-A226Y, comparing mutant versus wildtype at two corrected ages: 9 months and 15 months.
The workflow combines differential transcriptomics and metabolomics to identify pathway-level progression across time, with emphasis on bile acid metabolism, oxidative stress, lipid remodeling, and protein quality control pathways.

title: Integrated Transcriptome-Metabolome Analysis of Rps2-A226Y Mutant Liver
text:
Main Biological Takeaways

The mutant phenotype is progressive from 9m to 15m across both omics layers.
Bile acid pathway dysregulation strengthens with age and remains a dominant signature.
Stress-adaptation programs appear stronger earlier, with altered regulatory balance later.
Lipid and antioxidant pathway changes support age-dependent metabolic remodeling.
Most strongly significant features preserve direction across time, with selective switches.
Sphingomyelin species accumulate broadly, consistent with a chain-length-dependent ceramide synthase (Cers2/Cers4) shift toward the SM-conversion arm of the pathway.
Lysosomal genes, especially cathepsins, are broadly downregulated alongside XIAP upregulation, consistent with a lysosome-linked anti-apoptotic adaptation.
Pre-ranked GSEA (fgsea + MSigDB) independently recovers bile acid metabolism and proteasome/protein-degradation signatures among the top pathways.
Gene-metabolite concordance is not uniform across pathways: some (amino acid, purine/pyrimidine) agree in direction, while bile acid and lipid pathways show more disagreement worth further investigation.
A database-driven enrichment cross-check (SMPDB via MetaboAnalystR) is only weakly informative here: roughly 20% of measured metabolites appear in SMPDB, and that subset is biased against lipids. Correcting the statistical background from the pathway library to the measured metabolome weakens every contrast by about an order of magnitude, leaving no FDR-significant pathway at either age.
What remains is a nominal, uncorrected tendency toward depletion of TCA-adjacent intermediates and carnitine at 9 months, driven by a small overlapping metabolite set.

title: What Am I Currently Learning Professionally?
text:
In computational biology and translational data science, the ground shifts underneath your feet almost every quarter. Between new spatial multi-omics technologies, modern package managers, the realities of pharmaceutical R&D pipelines, and the rapid evolution of agentic AI workflows, a big part of my weekly routine is dedicated to structured learning and note-taking.
Recently, I looked back through my personal Notion LEARN and conference hubs to take stock of what I have been studying, testing, and refining professionally. Here is a synthesis of the six major tracks on my desk right now—plus the community events I am most excited to attend next and why I am deeply motivated to bring my ongoing research on tendinopathy and osteoarthritis (OA) across the finish line.

title: What Am I Currently Learning Professionally?
section: 1. Agentic AI, Guardrails, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP)
text:
1. Agentic AI, Guardrails, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP)
We have moved rapidly past the era of simply copy-pasting snippets into a chatbot. My recent focus has been understanding how AI coding agents actually operate under the hood—and how to use them in scientific computing without sacrificing rigor or reproducibility.

“You can use AI only to the extent where you can verify it.” — Terence Tao


The Mental Model: Agent = LLM + Harness + Tools + Loop
An AI agent isn’t magic; it is a language model placed inside a harness—a surrounding program that exposes read tools (listing files, reading code, querying databases) and write tools (editing files, running tests, executing shell commands) in an iterative observe \(\rightarrow\) act \(\rightarrow\) verify loop.


Beyond “Vibe Coding” to Disciplined AI-Assisted Development
In my notes, I draw a sharp line between vibe coding (prompting until something appears to work—fine for single-use prototypes) and disciplined agentic engineering:

AGENTS.md & Custom Skills: Maintaining explicit repository rules (AGENTS.md, R-coder.md) so coding agents immediately follow project conventions: keeping scripts modular (01_load_data, 02_qc_filter), separating /input/rawdata from /output/script_name/, and avoiding bloated defensive boilerplate on the first iteration.
Subagent Delegation: Using specialized subagents for isolated tasks (e.g., literature search, codebase exploration, or code review) to keep the primary reasoning context clean.
Model Context Protocol (MCP): Treating MCP as the universal connector (Host → Client → Server) that bridges LLMs with local tools, biomedical databases, and knowledge bases like Notion—while enforcing strict least-privilege and keeping API tokens out of git history and chat logs.







Hard-Won Lesson: Why Backups & Sandboxes Are Non-Negotiable



Giving an agent shell and filesystem write access carries real risk. In one memorable session, an agent was asked to back up a branch worktree before a history rewrite; due to a working-directory slip (cd failing silently), its cleanup step deleted the active branch directory instead of the duplicate! Daily filesystem snapshots saved the day—reinforcing why sandboxing, small reviewable diffs, and automated snapshots are mandatory when working with autonomous agents.




Scientific Literature & The Verification Burden
Following recent analyses in Nature on “Frankenstein citations” and Deep Research tools, another recurring theme in my notes is scientific accountability. While LLMs dramatically accelerate literature synthesis and code refactoring, they can still blend real author names with hallucinated DOIs or smooth over experimental nuances. In biomedical research, primary source verification remains strictly the scientist’s job.

title: What Am I Currently Learning Professionally?
section: 2. Pharmaceutical Lifecycle, Target Identification & Pipeline Strategy
text:
2. Pharmaceutical Lifecycle, Target Identification & Pipeline Strategy
Moving from academic discovery to industrial drug development changes how you look at a p-value. A major part of my recent professional learning has focused on understanding the end-to-end pharmaceutical R&D lifecycle—from early target discovery to portfolio strategy.

The Economics & Bottlenecks of First-in-Class Discovery
Bringing a novel, first-in-class therapeutic just to the threshold of clinical trials typically takes around 8 years and ~$1.3 billion in cumulative R&D investment. At the portfolio level, large pharmaceutical innovators must constantly balance franchise durability against patent expiry cycles: even when flagship medicines drive strong cash flow, long-term resilience depends entirely on launch cadence and replenishing the pipeline in high-conviction areas like immunology, neuroscience, and human genetics-backed targets.


Target Identification & The “Smoothing” Trap in AI Models
In early Target Identification (Target ID) and validation, we increasingly integrate bulk and single-cell RNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics, high-throughput affinity proteomics (e.g., SomaScan), and human genetic evidence. From recent industry deep-dives on Agentic AI for Drug Discovery, three practical lessons stood out:

Knowledge Graphs vs. GNN Smoothing: Biomedical knowledge graphs are indispensable for connecting targets, pathways, and clinical phenotypes. However, standard Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) tend to average and smooth node representations across neighborhoods—which can inadvertently wash out the exact individual outlier biomarker or rare cell-state signal that defines a druggable target.
Tabular Foundation Models for Single-Cell Scale: As patient-derived scRNA-seq atlases scale into millions of cells, emerging tabular foundation models offer promising ways to learn transferable representations across sparse, high-dimensional molecular tables.
Small Local Models for Proprietary Clinical Data: In pharma environments where patient privacy and IP governance are paramount, compact domain-tuned local models often beat massive external APIs for querying internal clinical and preclinical repositories.



Clinical Biomarkers & Patient Stratification
On the translational side, I have been learning how computational biologists partner with clinical teams and biostatisticians to solve real trial bottlenecks—such as identifying “fast progressor” biomarker signatures in Phase 2B clinical trials (e.g., in neurodegenerative and autoimmune cohorts). Success here is less about chasing the flashiest architecture and more about rigorous experimental design, handling longitudinal missingness, and ensuring signatures generalize across clinical sites.

title: What Am I Currently Learning Professionally?
text:
3. Programming, Environment Management & HPC Workflows
While R (Bioconductor, Seurat, limma, tidyverse) and Bash remain my daily drivers, I have been sharpening my cross-language tooling across Python, HPC clusters, and IDE ergonomics:

Fast Python Environments with uv: Moving away from slow Conda resolves toward uv (uv add -r requirements.txt, uv run python main.py) and executing reproducible parameterised notebooks directly from the CLI (uv run --active jupyter nbconvert --to html --execute ...).
R & Positron / VS Code Workflows:

Exploring Positron alongside RStudio and VS Code, mastering multi-cursor editing (Alt+Click, Ctrl+D, box selection) and custom keybindings on a Swiss QWERTZ layout.
Understanding S3 vs. S4 object systems in Bioconductor—balancing flexible data.frame/list workflows with formally validated S4 genomic containers.
Harmonizing multi-batch single-cell and bulk transcriptomics pipelines: automated mitochondrial/ribosomal QC metrics, consistent factor ordering across tissues, and deterministic color palettes (e.g., matching overlapping patient IDs across tissues using the glasbey palette).

UNIX & HPC Optimization: Configuring SSH ControlMaster multiplexing and disabling reverse DNS/GSSAPI bottlenecks for snappy cluster logins, managing UGE job scheduling, and bridging local Git/Bitbucket workflows with HPC environments.

title: What Am I Currently Learning Professionally?
text:
4. Machine Learning & Multi-Omics Statistical Foundations
As computational groups increasingly ask “What is our role when an LLM can draft the boilerplate code?” (a question recently highlighted by Fabian Theis’s group), the answer is clear: experimental design, statistical rigor, and biological interpretation.
Here are the statistical and ML concepts I have been revisiting and applying:

Multi-Study Omics Integration (MINT / mixOmics): Sequential two-step pipelines (batch-effect removal via ComBat followed by classification) often overfit and fail on external validation. I have been studying MINT (Multivariate INTegrative Method), which projects independent studies into a common latent space while applying \(L_1\) penalization to select sparse, reproducible biomarker signatures simultaneously.
Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) for Omics:

What’s not expressed matters: In RNA-seq, collecting zero-expression genes and running pathway enrichment on them is a powerful sanity check to see what biological programs are absent.
Thresholds & Transforms: Using median rather than mean thresholds when filtering low-count features, \(\log(x + 1)\) stabilization for overdispersed counts, and checking sex-specific markers and mito/ribo fractions early.

Ranking in GSEA (fgsea): Using the signed Wald statistic (\(\text{effect size} / \text{SE}\)) from DESeq2/limma rather than raw fold-changes to rank genes, ensuring both magnitude and estimation uncertainty inform pathway enrichment.
Stratified Evaluation & Core Metrics: Avoiding the classic ML trap of evaluating models on random time slices rather than stratified sampling across clinical covariates; keeping sharp distinctions between SD vs. SEM (\(\text{SD}/\sqrt{n}\)), Cohen’s \(d\) vs. Tukey’s \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\), Mann-Whitney U vs. Wilcoxon signed-rank, and Cosine Similarity (\(\frac{a \cdot b}{\|a\|\|b\|}\)) in embedding space.

title: What Am I Currently Learning Professionally?
section: 5. Why I’m Motivated to Finish My Research Project on Tendinopathy & Osteoarthritis (OA)
text:
5. Why I’m Motivated to Finish My Research Project on Tendinopathy & Osteoarthritis (OA)
Alongside my broader learning, one of my strongest personal and scientific goals right now is completing my multi-omics research project on human tendinopathy and osteoarthritis (OA)—integrating clinical knee replacement tissue cohorts, patient pain/functional metadata, histopathology, and transcriptomics/proteomics.
My motivation comes from two directions that reinforce each other every day: my personal life as an athlete and the thrilling scientific inflection point the musculoskeletal field has just reached.

Personal Connection: Sports, Trauma Rehab & Body Mechanics
Outside the lab, a huge part of my identity revolves around movement: climbing (including building my own home Beastmaker hangboard setup), mountain hiking, skiing, and yoga. Anyone who climbs hard or spends years in mountain sports eventually confronts tendon overload, joint micro-trauma, and the slow, humbling reality of connective tissue rehabilitation. Experiencing firsthand how mechanical load, rest, and progressive remodeling govern recovery gave me an enduring fascination with body mechanics—how physical force is translated into cellular decisions, and why some tissues heal cleanly while others spiral into chronic pain and degeneration.


Scientific Inspiration: Key Themes from EORS 2026
Attending the European Orthopaedic Research Society (EORS 2026) meeting recently crystallized just how much new biology we can now uncover in tendon and joint disease:

The Lifelong Clock of Low-Turnover Tissues: Radiocarbon-dating studies of human musculoskeletal tissues reveal a sobering truth: the core collagen matrix of adult tendon and articular cartilage formed by skeletal maturity (~age 17) experiences virtually zero turnover for the rest of our lives. Because adult tendons cannot simply rebuild their developmental scaffold from scratch, injury triggers fibrotic repair rather than true regeneration.
Fibroblast Subpopulations & How Fibrosis Actually Resolves: Single-cell and spatial profiling (highlighted in keynote work by Prof. Stephanie Dakin and colleagues) has shown that fibroblasts are far from uniform. In OA synovium, \(\text{FAP}^+\text{THY1}^-\) lining fibroblasts drive MMP-mediated cartilage destruction, while \(\text{FAP}^+\text{THY1}^+\) sublining fibroblasts drive inflammation and fibrosis. Even more inspiring is using frozen shoulder as a natural human model of self-limiting fibrosis: comparing persisting tendinopathy against resolving capsule fibrosis reveals that pro-resolving \(\text{MerTK}^+\) macrophages actively crosstalk with \(\text{DKK3}^+\) fibroblasts to dissolve fibrotic matrix—pointing toward pro-resolving therapies rather than blunt anti-inflammatories (like NSAIDs or glucocorticoids) that can impair tissue integrity.
Macrophage Network Plasticity & Emerging Tendon Axes: Dynamical systems modeling of macrophage polarization (~81-node regulatory networks) helps explain clinical paradoxes in OA: for instance, why \(\text{TGF-}\beta\) is essential for synovial homeostasis in health yet locks in stiffness and fibrosis in established OA, why \(\text{IL-1}\beta\) blockade alone fails to flip pro-inflammatory macrophage attractors, and how axes like hypoxia–glutamate signaling, JAK-STAT pathways, and mechanosensitive ion channels (Piezo1) govern pathological tendon remodeling.
Bridging \(2\,\mu\text{m}\) Spatial Omics with Biomechanical Strain: We are moving rapidly from \(50\,\mu\text{m}\) spot arrays to \(2\,\mu\text{m}\) single-cell spatial transcriptomics even in challenging calcified joint tissues—and registering 2D spatial gene expression directly onto 3D micro-CT and cyclic mechanical strain maps to see which genes switch on in high-strain vs. low-strain micro-niches.

Bringing these clinical, biomechanical, and multi-omics layers together in our own OA and tendinopathy datasets feels like solving a puzzle that matters both at the bench and on the climbing wall.

title: What Am I Currently Learning Professionally?
text:
6. Soft Skills, Scientific Storytelling & Toastmasters
Technical depth only creates impact when you can align people around it. In industry, where cross-functional teams of biologists, clinicians, biostatisticians, and executives have 15 minutes to make a portfolio decision, communication is a core multiplier.

Presentation Mastery at Toastmasters: I have been actively training at Toastmasters (completing levels in the Presentation Mastery pathway). Practicing in a supportive club environment has pushed me to be intentional about vocal variety (modulating pitch, volume, and pace rather than rushing through dense material), the power of the pause (letting a key insight land before moving on), stage presence & body language, and delivering structured, empathetic peer evaluations that balance encouragement with concrete, actionable feedback.
Coaching & Self-Leadership: Through professional coaching, I have been working on distinguishing what is within my direct control (my schedule, preparation, emotional pause before high-stakes decisions, and ownership mindset) from external organizational noise—and balancing technical “sprint” energy with long-term cross-team coordination.
Visual Hierarchy & Web Storytelling: Inspired by The Economist’s data visualization style guides, I focus on stripping away chart clutter so visual encodings match human perceptual hierarchy (position and length over area and color saturation)—and packaging complex findings into reproducible Quarto reports, Shiny apps, and interactive 3D web knowledge bases (built following the workflow shared by John Damask).

title: What Am I Currently Learning Professionally?
section: 7. Upcoming Events I’m Excited to Visit
text:
7. Upcoming Events I’m Excited to Visit
Learning doesn’t happen in isolation—it thrives in community. Two sets of upcoming events on my calendar that I am particularly excited about are:

Basel Spatial Omics Day & Single-Cell Community Meetups: Basel is a unique global hub where academic institutes (ETH D-BSSE, FMI, University of Basel) and pharma/biotech R&D campuses intersect. I am looking forward to Basel Spatial Omics Day to exchange practical lessons on high-resolution spatial transcriptomics, cell-cell neighborhood modeling, and tissue registration in complex human pathology.
Biomedical & AI Research Hackathons: After seeing how rapidly agentic AI workflows, MCP servers, and multimodal embeddings are evolving, I am eager to participate in upcoming Biomedical and AI Research Hackathons—collaborating under time pressure with engineers and domain scientists to turn raw biological datasets and knowledge graphs into working, verifiable prototypes.



Looking Ahead
Whether it is debugging an agentic workflow, modeling a Phase 2B biomarker signature, mapping fibroblast-macrophage crosstalk in an osteoarthritic joint, or stepping up to the lectern at Toastmasters, the thread connecting all of these tracks is curiosity paired with accountability: building tools and stories that hold up under real biological and clinical scrutiny.

title: Mounting the Beast: A DIY Guide to Installing a Beastmaker 1000 Hangboard
text:
Recently I started a full-time computational job and, to keep my body in shape, decided to place a climbing hangboard inside my apartment.
This is the story of how that decision became a reality, turning a blank wall above my doorway into a finger-strength training station. Here is the step-by-step saga of mounting a Beastmaker 1000 Series hangboard above a concrete door frame.


Step 1: The Blank Canvas
It all starts with a dream and a blank wall. The space above a doorway is ideal because it allows your legs and body to hang freely, but it is also a high-stress area. You cannot simply screw a hangboard directly into the plaster; you need a solid plan to anchor it safely.



The empty wall above the doorway—full of potential, but currently blank.





Step 2: The Foundation (Metolius Backing Board)
To avoid tearing down the wall and to distribute the forces evenly, we use a wooden backing board (in this case, a Metolius mounting board). This board is anchored securely into the solid wall structure, providing a stable, flat surface to screw the Beastmaker into.



The pre-drilled Metolius backing board, waiting to bridge the gap between the wall and the hangboard.





Step 3: Unboxing the Beast & Preparing the Power
With the backing board ready, it was time to open the main event: the Beastmaker 1000. Alongside the beautiful wooden board, I dug out my trusty Texmash TDU-1000 impact drill. A solid drill is non-negotiable when dealing with concrete or brick walls.



Unboxing the Beastmaker and prepping the Texmash TDU-1000 drill.





Step 4: Organizing the Arsenal
DIY projects live and die by preparation. I gathered the essential tools for the job: * A LUX-TOOLS 40 cm spirit level (crucial—nobody wants to train on a slanted board). * A utility knife for opening packages and clean cuts. * A masonry drill bit matching the anchor size. * A screwdriver and selection of screws.



Gathering the essential tools for a precise installation.





Step 5: Choosing the Right Anchors
When hanging your body weight (plus dynamic force) off a wall, cheap drywall screws won’t cut it. I opted for Fischer S 8x40 wall plugs (8mm diameter, 40mm depth) and matching heavy-duty black wood screws.

[!TIP] Always check the packaging recommendations. For the Fischer S 8x40, a hole depth of at least 50mm and an 8mm drill bit are required for maximum load capacity.




Fischer S 8x40 wall plugs and heavy-duty screws—the unsung heroes of this project.





Step 6: Making the Holes
With the backing board held up and leveled, I marked the drilling points. Then came the noisy, messy part: drilling the 12 anchor holes. You can see the neat little piles of concrete dust resting on top of the door frame, a testament to the Texmash’s impact mode.



Twelve clean holes drilled above the door frame. Measure twice, drill once!





Step 7: Inserting Anchors & Preparing Screws
Next, the Fischer wall plugs were tapped into the holes, and the long black screws were started. Having the screws partially inserted in the wall beforehand makes aligning and mounting the heavy wooden backing board much easier.



The screws aligned and ready to catch the backing board.





Step 8: Securing the Backing Board
The backing board is up! It went on smoothly and was screwed tight until it was completely flush with the wall. A quick check with the spirit level confirmed everything was perfectly horizontal.



The Metolius backing board is securely mounted and leveled.





Step 9: Unleashing the Beastmaker
Finally, the moment of truth. The Beastmaker 1000 was aligned on the backing board and screwed in using the wood screws provided. The wood-on-wood mount is incredibly strong and looks fantastic.



The finished setup: The Beastmaker 1000 is ready for training.


With the board solid as a rock, it was time to chalk up and test the 35-degree slopers. Let the training sessions begin!

title: A Knowledge Base for One Decision: Helping My Mother Choose an AMD Treatment
text:
My mother has age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Sooner or later, the conversation with her ophthalmologist will come down to a choice between two injected drugs: Vabysmo (faricimab) and Eylea (aflibercept). Both are given as injections into the eye, often for years, so the choice matters: it decides how often she has to come in for an injection, and how well the disease stays under control between visits.
I didn’t want to walk into that appointment knowing only the brand names. So I built a small website, the Macula Disease Knowledge Base, that collects what the clinical trials and recent reviews actually say, with every fact traced back to its source. It isn’t meant to replace her doctor. It’s meant to help us ask better questions.


The site
Here it is, live. You can browse it right inside this post, or open it in a new tab.

  


  The embedded site opens in its light theme; the toggle in its top-right corner switches to dark or to a Russian interface.

It has four parts:

Clinical trials: plain-language digests of the pivotal trials comparing faricimab with aflibercept: TENAYA & LUCERNE in wet AMD, and YOSEMITE & RHINE in diabetic macular oedema. Each card covers the design, the treatment arms, the exact posted outcomes and the safety.
Knowledge check: how AMD works and progresses, explained in layers from basic to molecular. It has hand-drawn diagrams of the eye and of the VEGF / Ang-2 signalling that these drugs target, plus self-check questions, in English and Russian.
Wiki: the core of the project. There are 43 pages on diseases, mechanisms, drugs and trials, and every statement cites the paper it came from.
Wiki map: a 3-D graph of how all those pages connect. Click any node to read the page.

How it’s built
I built it together with an AI coding assistant according to the tutorial kindly shared by John Damask after his public presentation on building research knowledge bases with AI. Kudos to that clear step-wise explanation! It follows strict rules about where knowledge is allowed to come from:

Sources go into a raw/ folder and are never edited. So far these are four recent open-access reviews (2024–2026): a broad clinical update, a review of the molecular mechanisms, a review of therapeutic options, and a perspective comparing faricimab with high-dose aflibercept.
The wiki is written from those sources only. Each page covers one idea, drug or trial, and every factual sentence ends with a citation to the source file it came from. When the assistant combines several sources into its own conclusion, that’s explicitly labelled as synthesis.
Contradictions are kept, not smoothed over. When two sources disagree, both claims stay on the page side by side. For example, one review credits omega-3 fatty acids for the 25% benefit of the AREDS2 eye vitamins, while another describes the formula with no omega-3 at all. These disagreements turned out to be some of the most useful findings, because they show exactly which numbers to double-check.
Open questions go into a research task list, to be answered later with new sources.

One command regenerates the website’s wiki and the 3-D map after every update. The whole site is static files hosted for free on GitHub Pages, and the source is on GitHub. I’ve since turned the setup into a reusable template, so I can start the same kind of knowledge base on any other topic in a minute.



What I’ve learned so far
From the evidence collected so far (summarised on the site’s decision page):

Both newer options keep vision as well as standard Eylea. In the TENAYA & LUCERNE trials, Vabysmo given up to every 16 weeks was non-inferior to Eylea 2 mg every 8 weeks. In the PULSAR trial, high-dose Eylea 8 mg given every 12 or 16 weeks was too.
The realistic gain is fewer injections, not better vision. About 45% of patients on Vabysmo were already on 16-week intervals after the first year.
Fewer injections matters in real life. Outside trials, patients often get fewer injections than they need, and vision suffers. Reviews call this the “durability gap”.
There’s no head-to-head trial of Vabysmo versus Eylea 8 mg. Both were tested against the same comparator, but never against each other, so any comparison between them is indirect.
The extra mechanism isn’t proven to matter yet. Vabysmo also blocks angiopoietin-2, which should stabilise blood vessels. But a phase 2 trial found no clear benefit from that part, and its longer intervals may partly come from the dose.
Safety looked similar in the trials. Neither drug caused more eye inflammation than standard Eylea.



Questions we’ll take to the ophthalmologist

How often would each option need to be injected for her, and how is the interval adjusted?
Which drugs are available and covered here, including Eylea 8 mg?
If fluid persists on one drug, is switching to the other an option?
What signs at home (e.g. on an Amsler grid) should prompt an earlier visit?




What’s next
The site’s task list already has the next questions: long-term (3-year) results and any head-to-head comparisons, real-world safety data since approval, and what happens when patients switch drugs. As I add sources, the wiki, the map and the site update together.
This is a family project to understand the evidence. It isn’t medical advice, and every treatment decision belongs with her ophthalmologist.
